summary: Garry Tan frames YC's transformation into an AI-native institution and argues that companies can now achieve output levels where one person does what formerly took a thousand. He opens with a personal data point: in 2013 he wrote about 14 usable logical lines of code per day; today, using AI agents, his output is approximately 400x. The same Claude model serves both 2x and 100x people—the leverage lies in how work is wired, not in the weights. Tan maps every part of a traditional organization onto AI-native artifacts: skill files are employees, resolver tables are org charts, filing rules are internal processes, and trigger evals are performance reviews. When founders use tools like Claude Code, they are hiring, training, and managing a workforce made of markdown. He cites Emergence and Retail as proof that revenue-per-head ratios are unprecedented. Tan distinguishes latent space (LLM domain of taste and judgment) from deterministic space (code), arguing most AI bugs arise when computation happens in the wrong space. Drawing on cognitive psychology's seven-plus-or-minus-two finding, he notes human working memory holds about seven items while AI agents hold roughly a million tokens. The company brain is therefore the library plus the librarian: context engineering determines which books are open on the agent's desk. Tan then describes his own GBrain—a 220,000-page personal brain, open source and MIT licensed, effectively Postgres for agents. When a founder emails him about a crisis, his agent already pulls prior conversations and relevant portfolio company data before he finishes reading. He stresses that the primitive is not memory but memory plus hygiene: provenance on every fact, contradiction checks, and a librarian whose job is pruning. An uncured brain becomes a garbage dump with great search. He prescribes the discipline of never doing one-off work—skillify every task so the organization compounds knowledge daily. Model quality is rented, but if you build your brain, you own it. Tan closes by calling founders to build AI-native companies from day one, noting every company on Earth will need a brain. He frames abundance not as policy but as shipped software, illustrated by a father who built an 80,000-file brain for his son's rare epilepsy. The final message: every archive too big to read, every dataset too gnarly to clean, every ocean you were told not to boil—we can boil the ocean now.

sections.title: Introduction: The AI Revolution and YC's Transformation
sections.summary: Tan introduces himself as founder, investor, and head of a 20-year-old institution becoming AI-native, stating that one person can now do what used to take a thousand people—mechanically, not metaphorically.

sections.title: The 400x Productivity Jump
sections.summary: Tan compares his 2013 output of 14 lines of code per day to today's 400x, deflating to 8x floor and 80x midpoint. He stresses that 2x and 100x people use the same Claude; leverage is in how you wire the work.

sections.title: Wiring the Work: Treating AI as a Workforce
sections.summary: Tan maps organizational components to AI artifacts: skill files as employees, resolver tables as org charts, filing rules as processes, trigger evals as performance reviews. Using Claude Code means hiring and managing a workforce made of markdown.

sections.title: Real-World Impact: Lean Teams at Unprecedented Scale
sections.summary: Tan cites Emergence and Retail as proof of unprecedented revenue-per-head ratios, and notes YC's own non-technical staff building skill files and cron jobs, including a finance person who collapsed 100 Excel workbooks into one app.

sections.title: Latent Space vs Deterministic Space
sections.summary: Tan distinguishes latent space (LLM: taste, judgment, non-deterministic calls) from deterministic space (code). Bugs arise when computation is in the wrong space. He illustrates with a Startup School seating problem for 800 people.

sections.title: Working Memory and the Company Brain
sections.summary: Tan contrasts human working memory (7 plus or minus 2 items) with AI agent capacity (1 million tokens, ~3 Harry Potter books). A company brain is the library plus the librarian; context engineering determines whether agents are geniuses or goldfish.

sections.title: Building GBrain: Managing Institutional Knowledge
sections.summary: Tan describes his personal GBrain—open source, MIT licensed, effectively Postgres for agents. It contains about 220,000 pages written mostly by agents from his email, meetings, and 20 years of notes. When a founder emails about a crisis, the agent pulls prior conversations and relevant portfolio data before Tan finishes reading. This is the difference between an assistant and a colleague.

sections.title: Failure Modes and Memory Hygiene
sections.summary: Tan stress-tests his own pitch: an uncured brain becomes a garbage dump with great search; retrieval surfaces stale facts with total confidence; a bad skill file encodes a bad process forever. The primitive is not memory but memory plus hygiene—provenance on every fact, contradiction checks, and a librarian whose job is pruning. Treat the brain as production infrastructure and it compounds.

sections.title: The Discipline of Skillifying Your Work
sections.summary: Tan prescribes never doing one-off work. When you finish a task with an AI agent and are happy with the output, skillify it—turn it into a reusable skill file. If you have to ask for something twice, you failed. Organizations that capture what they learn get smarter every day; those that don't wake up with amnesia. Model quality is rented, but if you build your brain, you own it.

sections.title: The Call to Build AI-Native Companies
sections.summary: Tan answers Theo's question directly: build the AI-native company, not one that merely uses AI. A thin team, skill files for everything, the founder still in the code, and a company brain. GBrain is open source and free, but Codex will do 90% of this. The concepts—skill files, the librarian, never doing one-off work—travel to any stack. Every company on Earth is about to need a brain.

sections.title: The Power of Abundance Through Shipped Software
sections.summary: Tan addresses fears about job loss as a failure of imagination. He tells of a father who built an 80,000-markdown-file brain for his son's rare epilepsy—no lab, no grant, no permission. Abundance is not a policy paper; it is shipped software. Every archive too big to read, every dataset too gnarly to clean, every ocean you were told not to boil—we can boil the ocean now.
